Chapter 2: Understanding the Stories We Tell Ourselves About Money
You know, money isn’t just about dollars and cents. It’s really shaped by the stories we pick up along the way, sometimes without even realizing it.
Maybe you grew up hearing that money’s always tight, and it’s something you have to worry about. Or maybe spending was treated like a reward, and talking about finances felt... well, a little impolite. These beliefs—often picked up quietly, just in the background—end up guiding our decisions for years.
Take someone who watched their parents argue about bills every single month. As an adult, they might get anxious every time a bill lands in their mailbox—even when they actually have enough to cover it. Or think about someone raised in a family where shopping was the go-to way to celebrate or deal with tough times. That person might find it almost impossible to say no to impulse buys, even as the debt piles up.
These patterns? They’re not just habits. They’re rooted deep, in beliefs about what money really means.
It’s so easy to overlook how much these stories shape our everyday lives. Most folks don’t even realize that the way they save, spend, or talk about money is often influenced by old memories or cultural expectations. Sometimes, sure, these beliefs help us—but honestly, a lot of the time, they hold us back. Think about it: telling yourself “I’m just bad with money” or “I’ll never get ahead” can end up becoming a sort of self-fulfilling prophecy.
There’s a story about a woman who was constantly frustrated by overdraft fees. She traced her habits all the way back to her teenage years, remembering how her parents would say, “Don’t worry about money, things will work out.” As an adult, that turned into avoiding financial planning altogether. It wasn’t until she noticed the connection that things started to change. She began to ask: Is it really true that things always work out without any effort? Little by little, she started taking small steps to manage her money more intentionally.
Now, changing these stories isn’t about blaming your parents or your past. It’s about noticing the patterns, and then deciding which ones actually help you today. Most of us are carrying at least one old belief about money that just doesn’t fit our current life. The first step to rewriting these stories? Get curious. Where did this idea come from? Is it helping, or is it holding you back?
With time, and a little self-reflection, you can let go of those old scripts and start creating new ones—ones that actually support your real goals and values.
